specAnchors.text: know that nuclear reactions, including fission, fusion and radioactive decay, can be a source of energy

primer.text: The nucleus is an energy vault: fusing small nuclei together, splitting large ones apart, or letting an unstable nucleus decay all open that vault and pour out energy. Stars run on fusion, power stations on fission, and every radioactive source leaks a little of the same store as it decays.

modules.title: Sources of nuclear energy and fusion
modules.opening: A nucleus packs away an enormous store of energy, and three kinds of reaction can release it: fusion, fission and radioactive decay. Fusion is the joining of two small nuclei into one larger nucleus — the reaction that lights the stars, where deuterium and tritium can merge into helium.
keyPoints: A nucleus holds a huge amount of energy that nuclear reactions can set free.
Fusion, fission and radioactive decay are the three sources of nuclear energy.
In fusion, two small nuclei join together and build one larger nucleus.
Deuterium and tritium, both isotopes of hydrogen, can fuse into a helium nucleus.
Fusion runs naturally in stars, but not in everyday conditions on Earth.

low.restatement: Fusion: two little nuclei become one bigger nucleus and give out energy.
low.analogy: Two small snowballs rolled into one bigger snowball — joining releases the squash.
low.examPointer: Learn the trio of nuclear energy sources — fusion, fission, decay — as one list.

medium.restatement: Fusion converts a sliver of mass into energy when light nuclei merge; deuterium and tritium are the classic hydrogen pair that produce helium.
medium.analogy: A crowded train carriage: squeezing two small groups into one seat-row releases shoving energy — the closer the packing, the bigger the release.
medium.examPointer: Quote the coal equivalence only as 'about ten million kilograms per kilogram of hydrogen' — it is an order-of-magnitude fact, not a precise conversion.

modules.title: Fission basics
modules.opening: Fission is the mirror image of fusion: one heavy nucleus divides into a pair of smaller ones. The splitting nucleus is called the parent and the pieces are the daughters, and this is the reaction that today's nuclear power stations use to make electricity.
keyPoints: Nuclear fission: a heavy parent nucleus divides into two smaller daughter nuclei.
The splitting nucleus is the parent; the fragments are the daughter nuclei.
Fission is the process nuclear power stations use to generate electricity.
Like fusion, fission releases energy stored in the nucleus.

low.restatement: Fission: one big nucleus breaks into two smaller pieces and releases energy.
low.analogy: A packed suitcase bursting open: the single case (parent) splits into two smaller bags (daughters) that fly apart.
low.examPointer: Keep parent and daughter straight: parent splits, daughters are produced.

medium.restatement: Fission divides a large parent nucleus into two daughter nuclei, releasing nuclear energy that power stations convert into electricity.
medium.analogy: Splitting a log: one heavy piece becomes two lighter pieces, and the stored tension in the wood is released as the halves spring apart.
medium.examPointer: Power-station questions usually want the words fission, parent and daughter used precisely — name them, don't paraphrase.

glossary.definition: Joining of two small nuclei into one larger nucleus, releasing energy.
Splitting of one large nucleus into two smaller daughter nuclei, releasing energy.
A hydrogen isotope whose nucleus carries one proton and one neutron; a fusion fuel.
A heavier hydrogen isotope that can fuse with deuterium to make helium.
